**Ercole Pietro Manfredi** (2 July 1883 – 9 June 1973) was an Italian architect who lived and worked in early twentieth-century Siam (now Thailand). Born in Turin, Italy, he attended the Albertina Academy of Fine Arts before travelling to Bangkok, where he was one of many Westerners employed by the Siamese government.
He made significant career progress through the court of King Vajiravudh, but left government office to work privately as the country was going through political change, which abolished absolute monarchy and decreased government employment of foreigners. However, by adopting a Thai identity and way of life, marrying a Thai woman and settling down permanently, Manfredi remained a relevant and respected figure in Thai architecture, and later became a lecturer at Chulalongkorn University. His works include various royal residences and public institutions, ranging in style from Venetian Gothic to modernist, and incorporated Thai traditional styles as well. He contributed to much of Bangkok's architectural heritage, but no complete records of his works were kept.

Ercole Pietro Manfredi was born on 2 July 1883 in Turin, Italy to Luigi Manfredi and Caterina Bo. He attended the Lagrange Royal Technical School starting in 1894 and the San Carlo Technical School from 1898 to 1899. At the age of sixteen, he was admitted into the Albertina Academy of Fine Arts, where, during his studies, he received a first prize in architecture, design, perspective and painting. He received a diploma in 1907 and subsequently attended the Higher Course in Architecture. During this time, he also worked for Turin's Public and Municipal Works Department, where he supervised constructions and patented an earthquake engineering system. In 1909, he graduated with a High Qualification as painter and architect, receiving a gold medal first prize in addition to fifteen other prizes won during his studies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-1)
In 1909, Manfredi was selected by the academy to fill an architect position for the government of Siam (now Thailand). Sailing from Genoa, he arrived in Bangkok on 1 December. He was placed under the Architectural Section of the Ministry of Public Works, working under engineer-in-chief Carlo Allegri and Minister Prince Nares Varariddhi. He collaborated with many Italian architects employed by the government, including Mario Tamagno, who was the department's chief architect, and others who were involved in the construction of Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall. Many of these architects were in fact also from Turin or alumni of Albertina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-2)

In 1912, Manfredi was promoted to a position in the Ministry of the Royal Household, where he worked closely with King Vajiravudh and Prince Narisara Nuvadtivongs. He was subsequently promoted to Chief Architect and third court officer in 1917 and first court officer in 1921. In 1920, he was appointed the post of naval architect, with the rank of lieutenant-commander in the Royal Naval Scout Corps, which was the king's private battalion in the Wild Tiger Corps paramilitary movement. He later became Chief Architect of the Archaeological Section of the Royal Institute in 1926. During his service to the government, he was decorated with the Order of the Crown of Siam (commander, 1913), the Dushdi Mala Medal for artistic merit (1915), and the Order of the White Elephant (commander, 1920). He was also awarded the gold medal prize at the Bangkok Fine Arts Exhibition in 1917.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-4-3)
In 1930, during the period of political turmoil leading up to the abolition of absolute monarchy in the Siamese Revolution of 1932, Manfredi retired from government office. For a while, he pursued archaeological studies as an assistant to the French archaeologist George Coedes. He then continued his work as an architect, privately cooperating with Christiani & Nielsen (Siam) Ltd. from 1934 to 1936 and the Impresitor Company from 1937 to 1938.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_4-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Noobanjong,_p._354-5)

In 1939, Manfredi became a lecturer at the Faculty of Architecture of Chulalongkorn University, where he taught for eight years. He also served as a lecturer in the Signalling Division of the Royal Thai Navy from 1944 to 1950 before retiring from public life.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-6)
While in Turin, Manfredi married his first wife, by whom he had two children—Luisa (1906–1990) and Gabriele (1914–2016)—both of whom would later become active in the partisan resistance against Mussolini during 1943–1945. Luisa would marry writer Robin Victor Lethbridge Raleigh-King in 1950.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-7)
In Siam, Manfredi adopted the local culture and way of life. He dressed and ate like a Thai, mingled with Thai friends, and used an abacus to calculate. His government contract had required him "to be able within one year to converse in Siamese in a tolerable way," but he went further and became fluent in both the spoken and written language.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_4-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-8)
Manfredi married a Thai wife, Thongmuan (Thai: ทองม้วน), with Buddhist rites in 1913, while his pregnant first wife returned to Italy. He and Thongmuan had two daughters and lived together in what he described as "years of paradise".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Amranand-9) He left the country only twice, in 1925 and 1928, to represent Siam at the second and third International Book Fairs in Florence.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-6)

Following the revolution of 1932, rising nationalistic sentiments resulted in a large decline in the role and numbers of Westerners working for the government. Manfredi was among the few who remained in Thailand. Like Corrado Feroci, he took up a Thai name, Ekkarit Manfendi (เอกฤทธิ์ หมั่นเฟ้นดี), and received Thai nationality on 29 November 1943. By adopting a Thai identity, he remained a relevant and respected figure in the Thai field of architecture.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-10)
Manfredi was involved in various humanitarian and cultural organisations. He was a member of the Siam and the Italian Red Cross, the Siam Teachers' Association, the Automobile Club of Siam, and the Alliance française. He also maintained links with his Italian roots, and was a member of the Dante Alighieri Society, the Colonial Italian Institute, and the Italian Touring Club. He was also selected as a correspondent member of the Italian Book Institute of Florence in 1929.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-4-3)

Manfredi has been described as rather eccentric for a foreigner in Siam at the time. In an interview, his daughter Maly Manfredi remarked that he was "an odd number".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-11) He was also noted to be impulsive and stubborn, often ignoring his wife's sensible advice to do what he wanted, including leaving his official post to pursue archaeology. According to Maly, "as court architect, he used to fly into a rage at the suppliers' gifts," and "Papa needed a big organisation to discipline him, like the Court or Chulalongkorn University."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-12) At the age of seventy-five, Manfredi realised his dream project of building a boat; to finance, he had to sell his entire collection of Siamese art. He named the boat _Mammino_, and used it mostly for pleasure cruises to Pattaya.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_9-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-14)
Manfredi lived in Thailand until his death on 9 June 1973. He and his wife (who died six years later) were interred at the Christian cemetery at Ban Pong, Ratchaburi.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_5-15)
Mrigadayavan Palace
Manfredi contributed to much of Bangkok's architecture and also produced works of painting and sculpture. However, he did not keep a record of his contributions, and his employment by the government means that many of his designs were not attributed. He also produced architectural works during his time in Turin, but his work during the brief period make up only a minority of his accomplishments.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_5-15)

Manfredi's architectural works involve both Thai and Western designs, which he adapted and developed to suit the local tradition.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_6-16) The more notable of these consist of royal palaces and villas; he also designed buildings for various public institutions.
Upon his arrival in Bangkok in 1909, Manfredi collaborated with other Italian architects in the construction of Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall, which had begun in 1908 and lasted until 1915. Manfredi was mainly responsible for the dome and the roof of the building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance and neoclassical styles and modelled in part after the Basilica of Superga. "Much of that copper covering the Hall, I put on with my own hands," he said in an interview with the _Bangkok Post_ in 1967. He also contributed to the decorations and was responsible for later work on the building's foundations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-18)
Thai Khu Fa Building of the Government House, formerly Villa Norasingh

He acted as chief architect for Mrigadayavan Palace in Cha-am and was in charge of its construction, which took place from 1923 to 1924. Designs for the seaside villa were sketched by King Vajiravudh and implemented by Manfredi. The palace consists of sixteen buildings and incorporates the Thai manner of elevated buildings with Western style and details.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_6-16)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-20) He also contributed to the design and construction of Villa Norasingh (1923–25), now the Thai Khu Fa Building of the Government House, although it is not officially attributed to him. The building was constructed mainly in the Venetian Gothic style and has a façade resembling that of Venice's [Ca' d'Oro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ca'_d'Oro "Ca' d'Oro"). He was not satisfied with the results, saying in a 1967 interview, "I built it in the Venetian style because I thought that Bangkok was the Venice of the East. Now I am so ashamed of it. It is not just right for this climate."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_7-21)

Manfredi produced many modernist designs in the 1930s. These include Manfredi Residence (1935) and Asawin Villa (c.1930s), which were influenced by the Bauhaus school and are among the first modernist buildings in Thailand.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Noobanjong,_p._354-5) The decade saw widespread adoption of the International style for public and educational institutions. Among these are Manfredi's designs for the Rajvithi School of Nursing (c.1930s) and the Chulalongkorn University Faculty of Dentistry (1939).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-22) Influences by the neoplastic (De Stijl) movement are seen in his designs for Triam Udom Suksa School (1934).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-23) He also designed Chulalongkorn University's Faculty of Fine Arts building, as well as the Chemistry and Physics buildings of the Faculty of Science.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_7-21)

While in Turin, Manfredi married his first wife, by whom he had two children—Luisa (1906–1990) and Gabriele (1914–2016)—both of whom would later become active in the partisan resistance against Mussolini during 1943–1945. Luisa would marry writer Robin Victor Lethbridge Raleigh-King in 1950.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-7)
In Siam, Manfredi adopted the local culture and way of life. He dressed and ate like a Thai, mingled with Thai friends, and used an abacus to calculate. His government contract had required him "to be able within one year to converse in Siamese in a tolerable way," but he went further and became fluent in both the spoken and written language.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_4-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-8)
Manfredi married a Thai wife, Thongmuan (Thai: ทองม้วน), with Buddhist rites in 1913, while his pregnant first wife returned to Italy. He and Thongmuan had two daughters and lived together in what he described as "years of paradise".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Amranand-9) He left the country only twice, in 1925 and 1928, to represent Siam at the second and third International Book Fairs in Florence.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-6)
texts.4:
Following the revolution of 1932, rising nationalistic sentiments resulted in a large decline in the role and numbers of Westerners working for the government. Manfredi was among the few who remained in Thailand. Like Corrado Feroci, he took up a Thai name, Ekkarit Manfendi (เอกฤทธิ์ หมั่นเฟ้นดี), and received Thai nationality on 29 November 1943. By adopting a Thai identity, he remained a relevant and respected figure in the Thai field of architecture.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-10)
Manfredi was involved in various humanitarian and cultural organisations. He was a member of the Siam and the Italian Red Cross, the Siam Teachers' Association, the Automobile Club of Siam, and the Alliance française. He also maintained links with his Italian roots, and was a member of the Dante Alighieri Society, the Colonial Italian Institute, and the Italian Touring Club. He was also selected as a correspondent member of the Italian Book Institute of Florence in 1929.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_3-4-3)
texts.5:
Manfredi has been described as rather eccentric for a foreigner in Siam at the time. In an interview, his daughter Maly Manfredi remarked that he was "an odd number".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-11) He was also noted to be impulsive and stubborn, often ignoring his wife's sensible advice to do what he wanted, including leaving his official post to pursue archaeology. According to Maly, "as court architect, he used to fly into a rage at the suppliers' gifts," and "Papa needed a big organisation to discipline him, like the Court or Chulalongkorn University."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-12) At the age of seventy-five, Manfredi realised his dream project of building a boat; to finance, he had to sell his entire collection of Siamese art. He named the boat _Mammino_, and used it mostly for pleasure cruises to Pattaya.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_9-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-14)
Manfredi lived in Thailand until his death on 9 June 1973. He and his wife (who died six years later) were interred at the Christian cemetery at Ban Pong, Ratchaburi.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_5-15)
Mrigadayavan Palace
Manfredi contributed to much of Bangkok's architecture and also produced works of painting and sculpture. However, he did not keep a record of his contributions, and his employment by the government means that many of his designs were not attributed. He also produced architectural works during his time in Turin, but his work during the brief period make up only a minority of his accomplishments.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_5-15)
texts.6:
Manfredi's architectural works involve both Thai and Western designs, which he adapted and developed to suit the local tradition.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_6-16) The more notable of these consist of royal palaces and villas; he also designed buildings for various public institutions.
Upon his arrival in Bangkok in 1909, Manfredi collaborated with other Italian architects in the construction of Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall, which had begun in 1908 and lasted until 1915. Manfredi was mainly responsible for the dome and the roof of the building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance and neoclassical styles and modelled in part after the Basilica of Superga. "Much of that copper covering the Hall, I put on with my own hands," he said in an interview with the _Bangkok Post_ in 1967. He also contributed to the decorations and was responsible for later work on the building's foundations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-18)
Thai Khu Fa Building of the Government House, formerly Villa Norasingh
texts.7: He acted as chief architect for Mrigadayavan Palace in Cha-am and was in charge of its construction, which took place from 1923 to 1924. Designs for the seaside villa were sketched by King Vajiravudh and implemented by Manfredi. The palace consists of sixteen buildings and incorporates the Thai manner of elevated buildings with Western style and details.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_6-16)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-20) He also contributed to the design and construction of Villa Norasingh (1923–25), now the Thai Khu Fa Building of the Government House, although it is not officially attributed to him. The building was constructed mainly in the Venetian Gothic style and has a façade resembling that of Venice's [Ca' d'Oro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ca'_d'Oro "Ca' d'Oro"). He was not satisfied with the results, saying in a 1967 interview, "I built it in the Venetian style because I thought that Bangkok was the Venice of the East. Now I am so ashamed of it. It is not just right for this climate."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_7-21)
texts.8:
Manfredi produced many modernist designs in the 1930s. These include Manfredi Residence (1935) and Asawin Villa (c.1930s), which were influenced by the Bauhaus school and are among the first modernist buildings in Thailand.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Noobanjong,_p._354-5) The decade saw widespread adoption of the International style for public and educational institutions. Among these are Manfredi's designs for the Rajvithi School of Nursing (c.1930s) and the Chulalongkorn University Faculty of Dentistry (1939).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-22) Influences by the neoplastic (De Stijl) movement are seen in his designs for Triam Udom Suksa School (1934).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-23) He also designed Chulalongkorn University's Faculty of Fine Arts building, as well as the Chemistry and Physics buildings of the Faculty of Science.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Manfredi#cite_note-Bressan_7-21)

Discover the places where The Beach (2000) was filmed in Thailand, including Bangkok and Phi Phi Leh Island.
* * *
Danny Boyle’s film of the Alex Garland novel was filmed on Hat Maya, the main beach of Phi Phi Leh Island, near Phuket, Thailand, amid allegations of ecological vandalism when imported palms were planted to make the ‘perfect’ beach even more perfect. The area was, of course, damaged by the terrible tsunami of 2004, but has now recovered from the disaster.
Phi Phi Island is reached by a daily passenger ferry from both Krabi and Phuket Pier (the journey time is approximately 90 minutes). Return tickets cost around 600 Baht. For 1,200 Baht per person, you can take a round-trip by speedboat.
Naïve traveller Richard (Leonardo DiCaprio) sets out to find the fabled beach from the bustling backpack melee of Khao San Road, downtown Bangkok.
The Beach location: the waterfall: Haeo Suwat Falls, Khao Yai National Park, Thailand | Photograph: Ivanushka / iStockphoto
The water fall is Haeo Suwat Falls in Khao Yai National Park, Thailand’s second-largest park. You’ll find the waterfall at the end of Thanarat Road in the center of the park. The park itself is about a three-hour drive from Bangkok, or there’s a bus service from Bangkok’s Northern Bus Terminal (Mo Chit) for Pak Chong and Nakhon Ratchasima about every half-hour. From Pak Chong and Nakhon, you can take a songtaew (a two-bench pick-up truck) to the park headquarters.
More scenes were filmed in Krabi and Phuket.

Movie Locations Guide

## Where Was The Beach Filmed? Discover Ko Phi Phi Le & Thailand's Iconic Movie Locations


## 2000


##  City Locations
Phuket, Bangkok (Thailand)

##  Location Types
Beach/Oceanview

##  Location Styles
Exotic/Tropical, Asian, Beachfront, Hostel, Sail

## About The Beach
The Beach is a 2000 adventure drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio as Richard, a young American backpacker in Thailand. When Richard hears a local discussing an idyllic and secluded beach, he sets off to find it. Accompanied by Francoise and Étienne, two French travelers whom he meets along the way, they discover the secret paradise of The Beach, located on an island in the middle of a shark-infested lagoon. The three join the community of people already living there and settle into island life. But as tensions mount between Richard and the other inhabitants, it becomes clear that all is not what it seems on The Beach.
The Beach was directed by Danny Boyle (Slumdog Millionaire) and written by John Hodge (Trainspotting) based on Alex Garland's novel of the same name. Upon its release, The Beach received mixed reviews from critics but was a moderate box office success.
To make sure that the pristine landscapes remained unspoiled during filming, Danny Boyle banned cigarettes from the set – even going so far as to hire someone to search through waste bins for discarded cigarette butts! This dedication to eco-friendly filmmaking made The Beach one of the first films to receive recognition from Greenpeace for its commitment to environmental protection during production.
A controversy arose during the filming process when 20th Century Fox decided to alter the natural beach setting of Ko Phi Phi Le by bulldozing and modifying it to give it a more "paradise-like" appearance. As part of the production process, some sand dunes were altered while coconut trees and grass were cleared to expand the beach. The studio earmarked funds to re-establish and restore the beach to its original state. However, environmentalists filed lawsuits claiming that the ecosystem was beyond repair, and the restoration efforts had been futile. After the completion of filming, a clear flat area with an odd distribution of trees was left at one end of the beach, which had been artificially created and was never corrected. Consequently, the whole region remained damaged from its original state until the tsunami of 2004.

## About The Beach
The Beach was shot primarily on the beautiful Thai island of Ko Phi Phi Le. Located in the stunning Krabi Province, it is part of an archipelago of six islands, which feature some of the most iconic limestone formations and lush rainforests in all of Thailand. With its majestic karsts jutting out from tropical foliage and soft white-sand beaches stretching along crystal-clear waters, it's no wonder why this paradise has been featured as a backdrop for numerous films over the years.
The majority of scenes in The Beach were filmed at various locations around Ko Phi Phi Le, including Nui Bay, a picturesque beach with soft sand and tranquil waters, and Laem Thong, a stunning stretch of beach with dramatic limestone formations along its shore. One of the most iconic scenes from The Beach was actually filmed at Maya Bay—a stunning bay surrounded by towering cliffs and lush vegetation—which has since become synonymous with the movie itself due to its popularity.
A trip to any one of these idyllic locations would be absolutely worthwhile for any fan of The Beach or anyone looking to experience some truly breathtaking sights in Thailand. With its pristine beaches framed by towering cliffs and vibrant green forests, Ko Phi Phi Le offers an unforgettable experience that is sure to provide plenty of lasting memories for years to come.

## Richard walking through the city streets scene in The Beach
Thanon Khao San, Talat Yot, Phra Nakhon, Bangkok 10200, Thailand
In Bangkok, Richard (Leonardo DiCaprio), a young American on a quest for adventure, makes his way through a vibrant and packed night market. The market is teeming with street vendors selling an array of items, and the surrounding ambiance is infused with the aroma of spices and food, inundating the senses. The cacophony of honking motorcycles and chatter fills the air.
Thanon Khao San, or Khao San Road, is a vibrant and bustling street in Bangkok, Thailand. It's a popular destination for backpackers and tourists alike, known for its nightlife scene and affordable accommodations. The street is lined with vendors selling everything from street food to souvenirs, and the atmosphere is electric with the sounds of live music and chatter. The energy is infectious, drawing in travelers from all over the world who are looking for a taste of Thailand's vibrant culture.
Tuk-tuks are a fun and unique way to get around Bangkok. They're essentially motorized rickshaws and can be found on most street corners. Negotiate the price with the driver before getting in and enjoy the ride. This filming location is right in the heart of Bangkok, so it’s easy to find.
Discover Filming Locations

## Richard meeting Daffy scene in The Beach
The Memory at On On Hotel, 19 Phangnga Rd, Talat Yai, Mueang Phuket District, Phuket 83000, Thailand
On Khao San Road, Richard lodges in an unremarkable travelers' hotel where he encounters Françoise (Virginie Ledoyen) and Étienne (Guillaume Canet), a young French couple. It's here that he also meets Daffy (Robert Carlyle), who informs him of an immaculate, untouched island in the Gulf of Thailand, which houses a hidden beach of extraordinary beauty. Daffy discloses that he had clandestinely settled on the island several years prior but left due to complications. Tragically, Daffy takes his own life, leaving behind a map of the island for Richard to discover.
Hotel scenes were filmed at The Memory at On On Hotel, a historic hotel located in the heart of Phuket Old Town, Thailand. Built-in 1929, this Sino-Portuguese-style building was originally known as On On Hotel and has been meticulously restored to its former glory. One of the standout features of the hotel is the beautiful courtyard, which is filled with lush greenery and tranquil water features. It's the perfect spot to relax and escape the hustle and bustle of the city.
This filming location is found in southern Thailand, close to the stunning beaches for which Phuket is famous.
Browse Video Shoot Locations

## Richard convinces the French couple to go to the island scene in The Beach
Surin Beach, Choeng Thale, Phuket 83110, Thailand
Once Richard acquires the hand-drawn map, he convinces Françoise and Étienne to journey with him to the island, and the trio depart for Koh Samui. While there, Richard crosses paths with two American surfers who have heard whispers of the island, and he provides them with a duplicate of the map.
Surin Beach, situated on the west coast of Phuket, is an exquisite and private beach. Boasting powdery white sand, crystal-clear waters, and lush greenery, it's no surprise that Surin Beach is frequently regarded as one of the most stunning beaches in Thailand. The beach is a favored destination for swimming, sunbathing, and indulging in water sports such as snorkeling, kayaking, and stand-up paddleboarding. The tranquil waters make it an optimal location for families with young children or individuals seeking a more serene swimming experience.
Throughout Phuket, taxis are an accessible mode of transportation to reach your intended destination. Inform the driver of your destination, and they will transport you directly to Surin Beach. This destination is about a 40-minute drive northwest from Old Town Phuket.
Film Shoot Locations Guide

## Boarding the boat scene in The Beach
Ao Por Pier, 3C6M+95Q Andaman Sea, Pa Klok, Thailand
Embarking on their private boat, a group of young adventurers set sail toward a secluded island. During the journey, Richard becomes smitten with Françoise . After swimming from a nearby island to their destination, they stumble upon a cannabis plantation, which is being protected by armed Thai farmers.
Nestled in the serene town of Pa Klol, Phuket Province, Thailand, Ao Por Pier is a picturesque pier. It serves as a popular departure point for boat excursions to neighboring islands and provides captivating vistas of the surrounding mountains and sea, making it an ideal haven for photography enthusiasts and sightseers alike. Visitors can savor the gentle sea breeze while taking a leisurely stroll along the wooden walkway or simply unwind on the pier, soaking in the calm maritime ambiance and watching the boats glide by.
Visitors can easily get to this destination by car, taxi or bus. It’s roughly a 40-minute drive northeast from the heart of Phuket.

## About The Beach
The Beach is a 2000 adventure drama film starring Leonardo DiCaprio as Richard, a young American backpacker in Thailand. When Richard hears a local discussing an idyllic and secluded beach, he sets off to find it. Accompanied by Francoise and Étienne, two French travelers whom he meets along the way, they discover the secret paradise of The Beach, located on an island in the middle of a shark-infested lagoon. The three join the community of people already living there and settle into island life. But as tensions mount between Richard and the other inhabitants, it becomes clear that all is not what it seems on The Beach.
The Beach was directed by Danny Boyle (Slumdog Millionaire) and written by John Hodge (Trainspotting) based on Alex Garland's novel of the same name. Upon its release, The Beach received mixed reviews from critics but was a moderate box office success.
To make sure that the pristine landscapes remained unspoiled during filming, Danny Boyle banned cigarettes from the set – even going so far as to hire someone to search through waste bins for discarded cigarette butts! This dedication to eco-friendly filmmaking made The Beach one of the first films to receive recognition from Greenpeace for its commitment to environmental protection during production.
A controversy arose during the filming process when 20th Century Fox decided to alter the natural beach setting of Ko Phi Phi Le by bulldozing and modifying it to give it a more "paradise-like" appearance. As part of the production process, some sand dunes were altered while coconut trees and grass were cleared to expand the beach. The studio earmarked funds to re-establish and restore the beach to its original state. However, environmentalists filed lawsuits claiming that the ecosystem was beyond repair, and the restoration efforts had been futile. After the completion of filming, a clear flat area with an odd distribution of trees was left at one end of the beach, which had been artificially created and was never corrected. Consequently, the whole region remained damaged from its original state until the tsunami of 2004.

## About The Beach
The Beach was shot primarily on the beautiful Thai island of Ko Phi Phi Le. Located in the stunning Krabi Province, it is part of an archipelago of six islands, which feature some of the most iconic limestone formations and lush rainforests in all of Thailand. With its majestic karsts jutting out from tropical foliage and soft white-sand beaches stretching along crystal-clear waters, it's no wonder why this paradise has been featured as a backdrop for numerous films over the years.
The majority of scenes in The Beach were filmed at various locations around Ko Phi Phi Le, including Nui Bay, a picturesque beach with soft sand and tranquil waters, and Laem Thong, a stunning stretch of beach with dramatic limestone formations along its shore. One of the most iconic scenes from The Beach was actually filmed at Maya Bay—a stunning bay surrounded by towering cliffs and lush vegetation—which has since become synonymous with the movie itself due to its popularity.
A trip to any one of these idyllic locations would be absolutely worthwhile for any fan of The Beach or anyone looking to experience some truly breathtaking sights in Thailand. With its pristine beaches framed by towering cliffs and vibrant green forests, Ko Phi Phi Le offers an unforgettable experience that is sure to provide plenty of lasting memories for years to come.

Haew Su Wat Waterfall is a breathtaking waterfall located in Khao Yai National Park, Thailand. As one of the most scenic and popular waterfalls in the park, Haew Su Wat attracts visitors from all over the world. The waterfall consists of three tiers, each with its own distinct character and charm. The first tier is the most accessible and is easily reached by following a short trail. The second tier requires a bit more effort but is well worth it, as it offers a spectacular view of the falls from above. The third tier is the most challenging to reach, and visitors must be prepared for a steep hike through dense jungle.
Visitors can take a bus to Pak Chong, the nearest town to Khao Yai National Park. From there, visitors can take a shared taxi or tuk-tuk to the park entrance, where they can follow the signs to the waterfall.

## Conclusion
The Beach is a well-known film that was shot in several beautiful locations across Thailand. The main setting of the movie is the spectacularly gorgeous shore of Ko Phi Phi Le, an island located in the southeastern region of Thailand. Throughout the film, viewers are treated to breathtaking views of lush jungles, pristine beaches, and crystal-clear waters. In addition to Ko Phi Phi Le, some scenes were also shot in Krabi Province and Bangkok.
The Beach perfectly captures the essence of Thai culture and nature. From its stunning visuals to its captivating storyline, this movie has become an instant classic amongst fans of adventure films and travel films alike. Audiences can’t help but be mesmerized by the exotic beauty depicted throughout every scene, from Richard’s journey to find “the perfect beach” to his interactions with locals on different islands around Thailand.
The end result is a captivating travelogue filled with unforgettable moments set against some of Southeast Asia's most beautiful natural landscapes. Whether you’re watching it for its picturesque visuals or for its dramatic plotline, The Beach is sure to leave you wanting more.
